_meta.description: A rough, original two-tier grouping of common produce items by how often multiple pesticide residues have historically been detected in USDA Pesticide Data Program (PDP) testing, used only to support AGGREGATE exposure awareness — i.e. what you eat most often matters far more than any single item. This is not a reproduction of any advocacy group's proprietary ranking, and detection of a residue does not mean it exceeded an EPA safety tolerance; the PDP itself reports the vast majority of tested samples are within tolerance.
_meta.methodology: Grouping reflects a well-established general pattern repeated across many years of USDA PDP annual summary reports (ams.usda.gov/datasets/pdp) and is intentionally coarse (two tiers, no ranking within tiers). Verify current-year specifics against the latest PDP report if it matters to you — this list is a starting heuristic, not a lab result for your food.
_meta.principle: Variety is the actual lever: eating the same few 'watch-list' items daily concentrates exposure to whatever residues they tend to carry. Rotating sources, washing/peeling, and not building a diet around any single produce item matters more than eliminating any one food.

watch_list.note: Thin skin, grown low to the ground; rinse well under running water.
Leafy greens have historically shown frequent multi-residue detections; washing and buying pre-washed doesn't fully remove residue but does help with surface debris.
Thin-skinned stone fruit; peeling removes more residue than rinsing alone but also removes fiber/nutrients — a personal tradeoff, not a requirement.
Thin skin, hard to peel practically; rinse well.
Thin skin; a produce-wash soak or peeling reduces residue if it's a priority for you.
Thin skin, eaten whole; rinse under running water (soaking helps more than a quick splash).
Thin skin, often minimal processing between field and table.
Thin skin; rinse well, especially if not organic.
Historically variable; rinsing before cooking helps.

Husk is removed and discarded before eating.
Outer papery layers are removed before use.
Thick skin, typically peeled before eating.
Fuzzy skin typically peeled or scooped, not eaten.
